accuracy.evidence: Checked against Met Office guidance ('How we measure temperature', 'How we measure rainfall', 'How we measure wind', the Beaufort wind force scale) and WMO Guide to Instruments and Methods of Observation (WMO-No. 8): thermometers in a white louvred Stevenson screen about 1.25 m above short grass, in the shade; rain gauges in an open site away from trees and buildings, rainfall reported as depth in mm; wind direction reported as the direction the wind blows from, which is where a vane's arrowhead points; cup anemometers spin faster in stronger wind and are sited at 10 m in the open. Beaufort descriptors used: under 6 km/h smoke drifts (force 1), 12–19 km/h leaves and small twigs in constant motion (force 3), 39–49 km/h large branches in motion (force 6). Equal rain depth in wide and narrow straight-sided pots follows from rain falling uniformly per unit area.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented children's ideas about weather measurement (Met Office education resources; Henriques 2002 on students' ideas about weather; primary teacher guidance on rain gauges): the vane points where the wind is going (step 2 predict 'East', vane wrong-direction message, Ana, p3, tag from), mixing up vane and anemometer (step 1 predict, Cara, Hal, tag vane), a wider container gets deeper rain (step 4 predict, m3, tag wide), not emptying the gauge and adding totals (Dan, Fred, p2, m9), and siting slips such as a gauge under a tree or a thermometer in the sun (step 6 predict, BADSPOT messages, Gus, p5, tags site and sun).

lab_distinct.evidence: gate_lab_distinct passed (under 30% similar to every flagship lab). The prerequisite lessons Temperature & Thermometers and Types of Weather (flagwxtype) cover reading a thermometer scale and naming weather; this lab instead turns a wind vane into wind arrows on a compass, maps anemometer km/h to Beaufort signs, rains on two pots of different widths, reads a millimetre rain-gauge scale with a draggable pointer and sites instruments in a garden. None of these mechanisms appears in another lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners discover the vane rule by acting: pointing the arrow downwind is rejected with 'That is where the wind is going', so 'into the wind' is learned from the feedback. Raining on a wide and a thin pot shows both water lines on one ruled line at 4, 8 and 12 mm, so 'rain is a depth' is seen before it is stated. The gauge task needs the pointer on the exact millimetre, and the siting task explains what each poor spot does to the reading.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions with tempting wrong options the task disproves: 'Wind vane' for wind speed, 'East' for a wind from the west, 'The wide pot' for deeper water, and 'Under a tree, so it is safe' for the rain gauge. The done message compares the learner's prediction with the result via A.reveal.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions with tagged wrong answers and their own messages: vane (vane shows direction, anemometer speed), from (winds named for where they come from), tool (each tool measures one thing), site (low, open, away from trees; a pole lets rain blow past), wide (same depth, more drops over a bigger floor) and sun (sunshine heats the thermometer). Lab errors name the slip too, e.g. 'Rain gauge under a tree: leaves catch the rain, so it reads too low.' and 'Close. The water is higher than 14 mm. Look straight across at the top of the water.'

readability.evidence: validate_lessons readability passed (kid under 6.5, adult under 9.5). Kid paragraphs are one tool each, with the precise terms thermometer, degrees Celsius, rain gauge, millimetres, wind vane and anemometer. Canvas instructions are one line per step and buttons say exactly what they do (Point West, Rain for 1 hour, Arrow up 1 mm, Check, Open grass).

no_filler.evidence: gate_content found no filler phrases and explanation similarity under 12% to all lessons. Every kid paragraph states what one tool measures, its unit and how to use or site it. The adult text gives curriculum links, Met Office siting facts, the six tasks and the named mistakes.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 screenshots of all eight steps before and after Show me (/workspace/wn-run-1116-2352/shots/wx-*): compass letters are 52×48 px tiles, rain-gauge scale numbers sit outside the tube, the five garden spots and three Beaufort rows span the width and stay above the feedback box, and the instrument drawings stay inside their cards. The challenge summary wraps 'Wind direction' onto two lines so it no longer overflows its card.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs passed on desktop and iPhone 13: all seven tasks complete with Show me, challenge shown, axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes, no console errors. Every drag has a button (four measure buttons, Point North/East/South/West, three Beaufort scenes, Rain for 1 hour, Arrow up/down 1 mm, Up 5 mm, Check, five garden spots, '<name> is right'), and the canvas aria-label states the wind arrows' direction, vane direction, pot depths, pointer reading and spots after each action.
